title: DWIT data migration & HIP integration transformation
summary: Defined the requirements, mappings and readiness evidence for wave-based migration to a cloud lakehouse and transformation of legacy interfaces onto the Hybrid Integration Platform.
challenge: The portfolio describes multiple legacy warehouses and around 2,000 point-to-point integrations, creating duplication, inconsistent data quality, support costs and scalability challenges. The Data Warehouse and Integration Transformation (DWIT) programme aimed to move warehouse data to a cloud-native lakehouse with Denodo virtualisation and legacy integrations to the Hybrid Integration Platform (HIP).
metricLabel: Migration scope, mappings and reconciliation evidence, as reported in the project portfolio
outcome: The portfolio reports a clear, auditable baseline linking business needs to build, testing and migration evidence. Phased scope, owned assumptions and evidence-based readiness decisions reduced the risk of late surprises in data history and downstream dependencies. It does not quantify savings or establish that every migration wave was completed.
facts: Facilitated discovery and architecture workshops with data, security, platform and integration specialists, engineers, product owners and operational users.
Built a migration requirements catalogue covering datasets, owners, history, frequency, volumes, retention, transformation rules and downstream consumers.
Produced source-to-target mappings, data dictionaries, lineage views and reconciliation rules with architects and engineers.

Assessed legacy interfaces for HIP onboarding, covering protocols, volumes, error handling, security, dependencies and ownership; defined API requirements, interface catalogue entries and service contracts.
Agreed each wave’s scope, historical period, cleansing rules, critical reports, reconciliation tolerances, rollback and sign-off owners.
Resolved a business–technical scope conflict through options analysis and phased scope with entry criteria for later waves.
Triaged late reconciliation variances into defects, approved transformations, source issues and tolerances approved by data owners.
Strengthened a supplier statement of work with measurable outcomes, acceptance owners, evidence-linked milestones and RAID ownership.
Managed RAID and traceability across DPS delivery teams; defined test conditions and supported SIT, migration testing, UAT, cutover and go-live readiness.
outputs: Requirements catalogue, traceability matrix, source-to-target mappings, business rules catalogue, interface catalogue, user stories with acceptance criteria, decision log, RAID log, UAT scripts and cutover checklist.
skills: Defined wave scope, history, reconciliation rules and tolerances.
Produced mappings, data dictionaries and lineage for lakehouse targets.
Assessed legacy interfaces and specified HIP onboarding requirements.
Linked functional, non-functional, security and migration requirements to tests.
Resolved scope and architecture-versus-delivery conflicts with evidence.
Defined ownership, lineage, quality controls and security requirements.
Strengthened the statement of work for acceptance and payment.
Supported SIT, migration testing, UAT and go-live sign-off.
framing: Summarised from the supplied project portfolio; not inferred from the CV.

title: Improving the DPS change-impacting process
summary: Standardised the data-change impacting process, strengthened quality checks and improved supplier engagement.
challenge: Data Platform Services change requests averaged 50 days to assess. Poor-quality supplier responses, incomplete requests and cost-query escalations delayed delivery across multiple teams.
metricLabel: Average impacting duration within six months, as reported in the project portfolio
outcome: The project portfolio reports a reduction in average impacting duration from 50 to 27 days within six months, a 25% improvement in project delivery timelines and fewer customer cost queries. These are reported outcomes, not independently audited measurements.
facts: Mapped the full process from Clarity requests and Jira tracking through architecture review, D&R documentation, walkthroughs, supplier impacting and consolidated responses.
Identified bottlenecks with technical business analysts, architects, engagement teams, suppliers and project teams; co-designed and embedded the future process.
Trained DPS colleagues to assess incoming requests for clarity, completeness and technical readiness.
Facilitated D&R walkthroughs and dependency meetings to identify impactors, risks, assumptions and constraints early.
Trained technical business analysts to consolidate supplier responses into coherent impact assessments.
outputs: Structured technical requirements, consolidated impact assessments, quality checks and process improvements.
skills: Introduced standard templates, QA gates and timed meetings.
Structured change requests into POD-aligned requirements.
Standardised statements of work and enforced SLA compliance.
Checked scope, RAID ownership and cost before customer response.
Coordinated walkthroughs and trained colleagues in QA and impact consolidation.
framing: Summarised from the supplied project portfolio; not inferred from the CV.
controls: Require adequate information; reject unclear or out-of-estate requests.
Standardise the template, baseline before issue and identify impactors up front.
Hold a walkthrough within three days of D&R and agree deliverables before impacting.
Hold a dependency and scheduling meeting within 5–10 working days of issue; assign issue owners.
Standardise supplier impact statements of work and enforce the 15-day SLA.
Technical BA and POD lead review scope, cost and RAID ownership before returning the assessment.

outputs: Validated requirements and process-mapping pack, gap analyses, procurement specifications and evaluation criteria.

Baselined current processes and co-designed digital workflows.
